articles.title: The Brighton collaboration standardized module for mpox vaccines, MVA-BN and LC16m8, benefit-risk assessment.
articles.summary: PMID: 43008353. DOI: 10.1016/j.vaccine.2026.129253. Based on the rapidly evolving multi-country outbreak in Africa, WHO declared mpox a Public Health Emergency of International Concern (PHEIC) from August 2024 to September 2025. In this outbreak, to date, over 100,000 suspected mpox cases and 1700 deaths have been reported from the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC). The MVA-BN and LC16m8 mpox vaccines have been recommended by WHO, the MVA-BN vaccine was WHO prequalified and the first shipment of donated vaccine arrived in DRC in Sept 2024. DRC launched the first phase of the mpox vaccination campaign in October 2024 with the MVA-BN vaccine and both vaccines have been used to help control the outbreak. The benefit-risk assessment (BRA) for the MVA-BN and LC16m8 mpox vaccines on "Myocarditis following MVA-BN, and the LC16m8 Mpox vaccines: A Case Study based on global data" was prepared by the authors on an urgent basis for the DRC national regulatory authority, the Congolese Pharmaceutical Regulatory Authority (ACOREP), in September 2024. The module was developed to help guide the utilization of the donated mpox vaccines in DRC and was prepared utilizing publicly available data from epidemiological studies, clinical trials, post-marketing studies and real-world evidence. The analysis was conducted for all WHO recommended schedules for the vaccines, including the MVA-BN vaccine administered subcutaneously and intradermally (as a dose-sparing option), for pre- and post-exposure prophylaxis, for adults and immunocompromised adults and LC16m8 vaccine administered to adults. The BRA was repeated in 2026 as there was additional data on the vaccines available. The base case of mpox incidence in the updated analysis was the annualized incidence of mpox reported in DRC from January 2024 through March 2025 (from the beginning to the main peak of the epidemic in DRC). High and low incidence were 10 x and 1/10 of the base rate, respectively, incidence rates that were considered so that the BRA is useful for different incidence rates during the outbreak, among different risk groups, and for different regions of the country. The results of the analysis were similar. The benefits of the MVA-BN vaccine administered subcutaneously or intradermally, for pre- and post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP), for children and adults, including immunocompromised individuals and one dose of LC16m8 vaccine administered to >1 year of age strongly outweighed the risks for the base and base x 10 incidence rates and marginally for the base/10 incidence rate. The updated analysis is presented in this publication.

articles.title: Immunogenicity and safety of two priming doses of an MF59-adjuvanted cell-based H5N8 influenza vaccine in healthy persons aged ≥18 years.
articles.summary: PMID: 42998534. DOI: 10.1016/j.vaccine.2026.129279. BackgroundIncreased transmission of avian influenza from animals to humans has elevated the risk of an H5 pandemic.MethodsThis phase 2, randomized, observer-blind, multi-center trial assessed the immunogenicity and safety of homologous priming with an MF59-adjuvanted, cell-based H5N8 A/Astrakhan/3212/2020 clade 2.3.4.4b vaccine (aH5N8c). We enrolled adults age ≥18 years, equally stratified into 18-64 (including a poultry-worker subset) and ≥65 year cohorts. Primary and secondary outcomes were homologous antibody responses against H5N8 measured in all participants by hemagglutination inhibition (HI) and in a subset by microneutralization (MN) assays on Days 1, 22, and 43. Solicited adverse events (AEs) were monitored for 7 days post-vaccination, with unsolicited AEs tracked throughout Day 43.Results239 participants were vaccinated (18-64 years, n = 121; ≥65 years, n = 118). At Day 43 (21 days post second aH5N8c dose), geometric mean fold increases (GMFI) were 13.7 for the 18-64 cohort and 10.2 for the ≥65 cohort. HI seroconversion rates were 75.8% (95% CI 66.1-83.8%) for the 18-64 cohort and 71.0% (61.1-79.6%) for the ≥65 cohort. HI titers ≥1:40 were achieved in 75.8% (66.1-83.8%) and 73.0% (63.2-81.4%) of participants, respectively. MN seroconversion rates were 80.6% (68.6-89.6%) and 70.0% (56.8-81.2%), while MN titers ≥1:40 were 83.9% (72.3-92.0%) and 86.7% (75.4-94.1%), respectively. No notable differences in immune responses by poultry worker status were observed. Most solicited AEs were mild or moderate, resolving within 3 days. Unsolicited AEs were reported by 16.7% participants by Day 43.ConclusionThese data support the use of the MF59-adjuvanted, cell-based monovalent H5N8 vaccine as a public health intervention against H5 influenza.

articles.title: COVID-19 vaccination and non-pharmaceutical interventions in selected European settings: a systematic review.
articles.summary: PMID: 43025126. DOI: 10.1016/j.vaccine.2026.129337. BackgroundCOVID-19 pandemic responses in European countries relied on both vaccination campaigns and non-pharmaceutical interventions (NPIs). While vaccination reduced severe disease, NPIs remained necessary to limit transmission, particularly during periods of variant emergence. However, the effectiveness of these strategies depended on social trust, communication clarity, and behavioural adaptation.ObjectiveTo synthesize empirical evidence on shared determinants of vaccination and NPI-related behaviours, behavioural relationships between these strategies, and evidence concerning their joint epidemiological effects.MethodsPubMed and Scopus were searched on 11 February 2025 using free-text terms for COVID-19, vaccination, and social or non-pharmaceutical measures. Eligible studies were peer-reviewed, empirical (quantitative, qualitative, or mixed-methods), conducted by authors affiliated with selected European institutions, and examined relationships between vaccination and NPIs. Studies based solely on modelling or secondary data were excluded. Data were synthesized narratively due to heterogeneity of study designs and outcomes.ResultsTwelve studies met inclusion criteria. Trust in scientific and governmental authorities consistently predicted adherence to NPIs and willingness to vaccinate. Sweden's reliance on voluntary measures was effective where institutional trust was high. In contrast, inconsistent communication in the United Kingdom contributed to reduced adherence and public frustration. Vaccinated individuals tended to increase social contacts, an association compatible with behavioural adaptation. A conjoint experiment examined stated vaccination preferences in relation to NPI attributes. Younger populations experienced notable psychological strain during prolonged restrictions.ConclusionsThe synthesis primarily informs social and behavioural relationships involving vaccination and NPIs. Shared determinants and behavioural associations should not be interpreted as evidence of synergistic effects on infection, hospitalisation, or mortality. Future pandemic preparedness should prioritize trust-building, consistent messaging, and targeted psychosocial support for vulnerable groups.

articles.title: Socio-spatial inequalities in routine childhood vaccination in Latin America and the Caribbean: a scoping review of territorial, social, and health service determinants.
articles.summary: PMID: 43033782. DOI: 10.1016/j.vaccine.2026.129356. BackgroundRoutine childhood vaccination inequalities in Latin America and the Caribbean (LAC) are shaped by social, territorial, and health-service conditions, but the evidence is dispersed across designs and scales.MethodsWe conducted a JBI-guided scoping review reported according to PRISMA-ScR. Six information sources were searched from inception through 15 August 2026 without language restrictions; the protocol was prospectively registered in OSF (10.17605/OSF.IO/ZSX6W).ResultsThe registered searches yielded 3251 records and 225 included reports; one additional eligible report was identified through other methods, giving 226 reports. Brazil contributed 126 reports (55.8%). Non-exclusive design features included cross-sectional/survey (69), ecological/administrative (49), cohort/longitudinal (21), spatial (18), qualitative (11), and explicit intervention/program-evaluation designs (9). Twenty-eight reports explicitly examined pandemic-related disruption or recovery. Socioeconomic gradients were not consistently monotonic, and direct Caribbean evidence was sparse.ConclusionsThe literature maps substantial socio-spatial heterogeneity in childhood vaccination but does not support a single causal hierarchy of determinants. More geographically balanced research using explicit equity stratification and evaluative designs is needed.

articles.title: Changes in childhood vaccination coverage and sociodemographic determinants across Nigerian states, 2018-2024.
articles.summary: PMID: 42998535. DOI: 10.1016/j.vaccine.2026.129317. BackgroundNigeria accounts for a substantial share of the world's zero-dose children and exhibits marked subnational disparities in childhood vaccination coverage. Although national estimates indicate modest gains in full vaccination, less is known about how vaccination outcomes and their determinants have changed across states over time, particularly following the COVID-19 pandemic. This study examines factors associated with changes in full vaccination coverage and zero-dose prevalence across Nigerian states between 2018 and 2024.MethodsWe conducted a repeated cross-sectional, state-level ecological analysis using data from the Nigeria Demographic and Health Surveys conducted in 2018 and 2024. Outcomes were full vaccination coverage and zero-dose prevalence among children aged 12-23 months. State-level sociodemographic, governance, and health system indicators were drawn from survey, administrative, and budget data. Ordinary least squares regression models assessed cross-sectional associations and relationships between changes in vaccination outcomes and explanatory variables over time.ResultsMean full vaccination coverage increased from 33.0% in 2018 to 40.8% in 2024, while zero-dose prevalence rose from 14.1% to 24.2%. Geographic disparities persisted, with states experiencing high zero-dose prevalence in 2024 often showing the largest increases since 2018. Maternal education was consistently associated with higher full vaccination coverage and lower zero-dose prevalence. In 2024, higher state health budgets, greater trust in local government, and COVID-19-related service disruptions were associated with higher full vaccination coverage.ConclusionsDespite modest national gains, zero-dose prevalence increased and disparities widened. Institutional factors appear increasingly important, underscoring the need for targeted, state-specific strategies to reach zero-dose children.

articles.title: Estimating the global and regional impact of introducing typhoid conjugate vaccination schedules: a modelling study.
articles.summary: PMID: 43044464. DOI: 10.1016/j.vaccine.2026.129352. BackgroundIn 2018, WHO recommended single-dose typhoid conjugate vaccines (TCVs) for typhoid-endemic countries. Emerging evidence of waning immunity has raised questions about optimal vaccination age and booster doses. A follow-up multi-model study evaluated vaccination schedules, focusing on booster strategies. Here, we expand findings from one of four modelling groups, estimating the global and regional health impact of TCV schedules.MethodologyWe developed an agent-based typhoid transmission model using the open-source Starsim toolbox. The model captures subclinical and acute infections, chronic carriers, and natural and vaccine-derived immunity, with age- and sex-specific parameters and outcomes. The model was calibrated to three incidence archetypes (medium, high, and very high) and two vaccine-derived immunity durations (fast and slow waning). Countries were mapped to archetypes based on national typhoid burden. We compared no vaccination with four strategies: routine vaccination at 9 months, 9 months with a booster at 5 years, 2 years, and 5 years, each with a catch-up campaign. Cases, deaths, and DALYs averted were estimated globally and across GBD super-regions over 10 years.ResultsGlobally, up to 29.5 million cases and 8.2 million DALYs could be averted with routine vaccination at 9 months plus a 5-year booster. Earlier vaccination and longer-lasting immunity generally increased impact. Under fast waning, vaccination at 2 years averted more cases and DALYs than vaccination at 9 months or 5 years, particularly in high-incidence settings where burden was greatest among children aged 2-<5 years. Boosters provided additional benefits, especially with fast waning. South Asia accounted for the largest share of global impact, followed by Sub-Saharan Africa.ConclusionTCV could avert substantial typhoid burden. The optimal age for a single dose depends on how quickly protection wanes, and boosters add benefit where waning is rapid. Better evidence on the protection duration, and country-specific analyses, are needed to guide schedule choices.

articles.title: Effectiveness of the 2025-2026 Covid-19 vaccine against Covid-19-associated emergency department visits and hospitalizations among U.S. veterans: An observational study.
articles.summary: PMID: 43002871. DOI: 10.1016/j.vaccine.2026.129254. BackgroundSARS-CoV-2 continues to cause clinically important morbidity, but Covid-19 vaccine effectiveness can vary across seasons as circulating variants, vaccine antigen composition, population immunity, and immunization policy change. During 2025-2026, peak Covid-19 hospitalization rates were lower than in the preceding season, making the absolute benefit of vaccination especially important for clinical and policy decisions. We estimated the effectiveness of the 2025-2026 Covid-19 vaccine against Covid-19-associated emergency department visits and hospitalizations among US veterans.MethodsWe emulated a target trial using electronic health records from the US Department of Veterans Affairs. Adults aged 18 years or older who received a 2025-2026 seasonal influenza vaccine between Sept 21, 2025, and Jan 31, 2026, were eligible. Same-day coadministration of the 2025-2026 Covid-19 and influenza vaccines was compared with influenza vaccination alone; recipients of influenza vaccine alone were censored if they subsequently received a 2025-2026 Covid-19 vaccine. Outcomes were Covid-19-associated emergency department visit, Covid-19-associated hospitalization, and their composite. Per-protocol vaccine effectiveness and risk differences per 10,000 persons at 180 days were estimated with inverse-probability-of-treatment-weighted and inverse-probability-of-censoring-weighted discrete-time survival models.FindingsAmong 931,943 participants, 114,911 received same-day Covid-19 and influenza vaccines and 817,032 received influenza vaccine alone. Over 180 days, Covid-19 vaccination was associated with lower risks of Covid-19-associated emergency department visits (vaccine effectiveness 31.72%, 95% CI 17.58 to 43.03; risk difference - 7.04 per 10,000 persons, 95% CI -10.34 to -3.63), Covid-19-associated hospitalizations (vaccine effectiveness 43.57%, 95% CI 16.12 to 62.10; risk difference - 2.63 per 10,000 persons, 95% CI -4.52 to -0.83), and the composite outcome (vaccine effectiveness 32.72%, 95% CI 18.94 to 43.82; risk difference - 7.41 per 10,000 persons, 95% CI -10.75 to -3.99).InterpretationIn this national cohort of US veterans presenting for seasonal influenza vaccination, receipt of the 2025-2026 Covid-19 vaccine was associated with lower risks of Covid-19-associated emergency department visits and hospitalizations. Absolute risk reductions were modest, but they quantify the benefit of vaccination in a lower-incidence season and can inform shared clinical decision making and seasonal vaccine policy.FundingUS Department of Veterans Affairs.

articles.title: Strengthening catch-up vaccination delivery in routine health services for children under five in Western Kenya, 2022-2024.
articles.summary: PMID: 43008350. DOI: 10.1016/j.vaccine.2026.129330. BackgroundCatch-up vaccination can close population immunity gaps, yet integration into routine immunization services remains limited in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). Following Kenya's 2023 catch-up vaccination policy, we evaluated a multi-strategy intervention to strengthen systematic identification, eligibility screening, and delivery of missed doses within routine health services in Siaya County.MethodsOver 12 months, five strategies addressing healthcare worker (HCW) capacity, vaccination documentation, defaulter tracking, immunization screening, and caregiver engagement were implemented in 55 public health facilities selected through stratified random sampling. Using a pre-post design, we assessed immunization uptake, missed opportunities for vaccination (MOVs), and system readiness. Baseline (November 2022-January 2023) and endline (October-December 2024) evaluations included facility assessments, HCW interviews, caregiver exit surveys among children aged <36 months with home-based records (HBRs; n = 658), and facility immunization register abstractions (n = 1650 children aged 12-23 months). Analyses accounted for sampling design, clustering, and used generalized estimating equations for HBR data.ResultsMOV prevalence among children visiting facilities for any reason declined from 94.4% to 20.9% (p < 0.001). Full immunization among children aged 12-23 months increased from 44.9% to 63.6% (p < 0.001), with uptake improving across antigens. Measles-rubella first-dose uptake increased from 51.5% to 78.0%, and second-dose uptake from 18.8% to 36.9% (p < 0.001 for both). Eligibility screening expanded from 60.6% to 86.8% of facilities (p = 0.012), defaulter tracking improved from 48.5% to 91.6% (p < 0.001), and HCW knowledge and confidence increased significantly.ConclusionThe multi-strategy intervention was associated with fewer MOVs and improved uptake, suggesting that embedding catch-up vaccination within routine health services can strengthen immunization systems in decentralized LMIC contexts. Kenya's catch-up vaccination policy provided a framework for introducing catch-up vaccination into routine health services.

articles.title: Pneumococcal vaccination coverage among adults aged 18-64 years at risk and aged ≥65 years in the United States - behavioral risk factor surveillance system 2024.
articles.summary: PMID: 43033783. DOI: 10.1016/j.vaccine.2026.129355. IntroductionPneumococcal disease, including invasive disease and non-bacteremic pneumonia, causes substantial morbidity among older U.S. adults and those with certain underlying medical conditions. We assessed pneumococcal vaccination and associated factors among adults aged 18-64 years with pneumococcal risk conditions and adults aged ≥65 years using 2024 Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System (BRFSS) data.MethodsWe conducted a cross-sectional analysis. Adults aged 18-64 years were classified as having risk conditions if they reported ≥1 prespecified pneumococcal risk condition or current/former smoking. The primary outcome was self-reported lifetime receipt of any pneumococcal vaccine; BRFSS did not collect product, dose, timing, or complete vaccination history. Weighted coverage estimates and adjusted prevalence ratios were calculated by sociodemographic and access-to-care characteristics.ResultsCoverage was 34.1% among adults aged 18-64 years with risk conditions and 70.3% among adults aged ≥65 years. Among adults aged ≥65 years, coverage was higher for those with risk conditions (74.6%) than for those without (63.4%) (p < 0.05). Coverage was 50.1% among all adults aged ≥50 years. In adjusted analyses, coverage was lower among Hispanic adults aged 18-64 years with risk conditions and non-Hispanic Black adults aged ≥65 years than among respective non-Hispanic White adults.ConclusionsSelf-reported receipt of any pneumococcal vaccine was 34.1% among adults <65 years with risk conditions and 70.3% among all adults aged ≥65 years. Improving healthcare access and engagement may improve vaccination. These estimates provide a baseline for evaluating expanded recommendations for all adults aged ≥50 years issued in late 2024 but do not represent current recommendation-concordant coverage.

articles.title: Hepatitis A vaccination coverage among adolescents aged 13-17 years, United States, 2024.
articles.summary: PMID: 43019905. DOI: 10.1016/j.vaccine.2026.129343. BackgroundHepatitis A is a vaccine-preventable viral disease that causes inflammation of the liver. The Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP) incrementally expanded childhood hepatitis A (HepA) vaccine recommendations from 1996 to 2006, the year when universal childhood vaccination was recommended. In 2020, ACIP recommended catch-up vaccination for children and adolescents aged 2-18 years who had not previously received HepA vaccine at any age.MethodsWe analyzed data from the National Immunization Survey-Teen (NIS-Teen) to assess HepA series initiation (1-dose) and completion (≥ 2-doses) among adolescents aged 13-17 years in the United States during 2024, identify factors associated with HepA series completion among adolescents, and evaluate changes in HepA vaccination coverage among adolescents since the 2020 ACIP catch-up vaccination recommendation by comparing NIS-Teen data from 2019 to data from 2024.ResultsIn 2024, national HepA vaccination coverage among adolescents was 91.8% (95% CI, 91.1%, 92.5%) for series initiation and 87.1% (95% CI, 86.1%, 88.0%) for series completion. Jurisdiction-level ≥ 2-dose coverage ranged from a low of 71.2% in Mississippi (95% CI, 63.9%, 77.6%) to a high of 97.5% in Georgia (95% CI, 93.4%, 99.1%). Adolescents who received an 11-12-year-old well child exam or checkup, saw a physician at least once during the past 12 months, had a mother aged ≥45 years, or had a mother with at least some college education were significantly more likely to have received ≥2 doses of HepA vaccine. Compared to 2019, significant increases occurred among U.S. adolescents in both HepA series initiation (7.4 percentage point [pct pt] increase in 1-dose coverage) and series completion (9.9 pct pt increase in ≥2-dose coverage) in 2024 (p < .05).ConclusionHepA vaccination coverage improved among U.S. adolescents following the introduction of the 2020 ACIP catch-up vaccination recommendation.

articles.summary: PMID: 43008352. DOI: 10.1016/j.vaccine.2026.129342. articles.title: School-based measles vaccination screening and catch-up program implementation in Zambia: costing study.
articles.summary: PMID: 43033784. DOI: 10.1016/j.vaccine.2026.129334. Many children in Zambia miss measles vaccination through routine immunization, while supplementary immunization activities (SIAs) targeting children under five may not reach older under-vaccinated children. School-based vaccination screening and catch-up (SVS) is a recommended strategy to identify and vaccinate these children, but evidence on its implementation and cost in sub-Saharan Africa is limited. We estimated the cost of an SVS pilot for measles vaccination in Zambia to inform implementation and potential scale-up. We conducted an ingredients-based costing from the Government of Zambia perspective of an SVS pilot in 20 urban schools in Lusaka and rural schools in Masaiti. Costs were estimated under three scenarios: base case (full pilot costs); post-introduction (excluding start-up and technical support); and budgeting (assuming full program integration and excluding start-up, technical support, and Ministry of Health and Education staff costs). One-way and probabilistic sensitivity analyses were conducted. Costs are reported in 2024 USD and Zambian kwacha (ZMW). Among 3351 children screened, 215 were identified as measles-rubella (MR) zero-dose and 211 were vaccinated. Total implementation cost was USD 75,886 (ZMW 2,111,157) in the base case. By input, personnel accounted for 70.6% of costs. By SVS activity, coordination and training accounted for 46.8% and 34.0% of total costs, respectively. Costs decreased by 28.3% in the post-introduction and 42.4% in the budgeting scenario. Cost per child screened was USD 13.05-22.65, and cost per MR zero-dose child vaccinated was USD 208.29-360.70. Coordination time was the most influential parameter. While costs per child are relatively high, SVS is a targeted strategy that can be used to reach older children who remain unreached by routine immunization programs and SIAs. Efficiency could improve through streamlined documentation, integration with school health activities, and reduced coordination and personnel requirements. Further research should assess its comparative value and cost-effectiveness against other approaches.

articles.title: Targeting T follicular helper (Tfh) Cells for Improved Vaccine Efficacy: Lessons from Diverse Disease Models.
articles.summary: PMID: 43050926. DOI: 10.1016/j.vaccine.2026.129357. Despite remarkable progress in vaccinology, many vaccines fail to generate durable and broadly protective immunity against rapidly evolving and deadly pathogens. Conventional vaccine strategies often rely on quantifying antibody titers or neutralizing antibodies, but accumulating evidence suggests that humoral responses alone may not ensure long-term protection. An effective vaccine must engage multiple components of the immune system, harnessing intricate cellular interactions to generate durable immunological memory. Among these, CD4+ T follicular helper (Tfh) cells have emerged as central players in orchestrating germinal center (GC) dynamics, where they provide essential signals to B cells for affinity maturation, class switching, and differentiation into memory B cells and long-lived plasma cells. Tfh cells thus directly shape the magnitude and quality of vaccine-induced antibody responses. The recombinant virus eliciting gC- and AnHV-1-specific antibodies with measurable virus-neutralizing activity.
